questions.q: Users see nginx's "502 Bad Gateway" page. Symfony's log shows no errors for that time. What is the most likely cause?
questions.hint: Who sent the answer: the app, or someone in front of it?

options.text: An exception in a controller
options.why: Then the app itself would have answered, with a 500, and the stack trace would be in the log.

options.text: PHP-FPM or the app server is down, so the proxy in front can't connect
options.why: A 502 means the proxy in the middle got no connection or no valid answer from the server behind it. The request never reached the code, which is why the log is empty.

options.text: A wrong DNS record
options.why: With wrong DNS the browser would never reach the server, so there would be no nginx 502 page to see.

options.text: The users' internet connection is bad
options.why: With no connection no response would come at all. A 502 page arrived, so the request did reach the server's door.

questions.q: In which of these failures will the Symfony app's log show nothing at all?
questions.hint: In which cases does the request never reach your code?

options.text: The domain's DNS record was deleted
options.why: The browser can't find the server's address, so no request reaches the app.

options.text: All of the load balancer's health checks fail and it returns 503
options.why: The load balancer is answering by itself; requests are not being sent to the app server at all.

options.text: A method is called on null inside a controller
options.why: That is an exception inside the app. Symfony returns a 500 and writes the full stack trace to the log.

options.text: Mobile data is switched off on the user's phone
options.why: The request never leaves the phone, so no hop on the server side sees anything.

questions.q: If a gateway returns a 502 with an HTML body, what happens in the Vue code below?
questions.hint: The body of a 502 page is not JSON. Which line runs first?

options.text: fetch itself sees the 502 and throws an exception
options.why: fetch throws only when no response arrives. A 502 is a valid response, so nothing is thrown.

options.text: res.json() throws a SyntaxError trying to parse HTML, and showError is never reached
options.why: The JSON is read before the status is checked. Check res.ok first, then read the body.

options.text: data.message will contain "Bad Gateway"
options.why: An HTML page can't be read as JSON, so data is never created.

options.text: The code is fine
options.why: It only works when errors also arrive as JSON. Machines in the middle of the road don't follow that rule.

questions.q: Kevin put a load balancer in front of his app. Since then his IP-based rate limiter blocks all users at once every few minutes. Why?
questions.hint: Whose IP does Symfony see now?

options.text: The rate limiter's limit is set too low
options.why: The limit is what it was before. What changed is that everyone is now counted as one person.

options.text: The load balancer sends every request twice
options.why: A load balancer doesn't duplicate requests. It just forwards them from its own IP.

options.text: Every request seems to come from the load balancer's IP, because trusted_proxies isn't set up
options.why: With everyone sharing one IP, all requests are counted in the same bucket. With trusted_proxies set, Symfony takes the real IP from X-Forwarded-For.

options.text: The database is running out of connections
options.why: That would show up as a 500 or 503, not as the rate limiter's 429.

questions.q: After the DNS record was changed to the new server's IP, some users were still reaching the old server half an hour later. Why?
questions.hint: Is the DNS answer asked for afresh every time?

options.text: Old DNS answers stay cached until the TTL runs out
options.why: Browsers, operating systems and internet providers remember a DNS answer for the TTL; until then they don't ask for the new address.

options.text: The load balancer is using sticky sessions
options.why: Sticky sessions are about choosing a server behind one load balancer. Here users are going to the wrong address in the first place.

options.text: Symfony's cache has not been cleared
options.why: Which server a user reaches is decided long before the app is involved. The app's cache plays no part.

options.text: Those users have old browsers
options.why: New or old, every browser caches a DNS answer for the TTL.

questions.q: A user stared at a spinner for 60 seconds and then got a 504. Which statements are correct?
questions.hint: Who sends a 504? And what happens to the code behind it after it gives up?

options.text: The answer came from the load balancer or gateway, not the app
options.why: A 504 means the proxy in the middle waited for the server behind it until its time limit ran out.

options.text: The app or its database was very slow
options.why: A 504 happens when the server behind the proxy doesn't answer in time, usually because of a slow query or a slow external service.

options.text: The work definitely wasn't done, so it is safe to resend it
options.why: Even after the proxy gives up, the app may finish the job. The outcome is unknown, and blindly resending can do it twice.

options.text: DNS returned the wrong address
options.why: With wrong DNS you would never have reached the load balancer, and no 504 would have come back.

questions.q: Which of these changes put old clients at risk of breaking?
questions.hint: What will the old client look for, and is it still exactly where it was?

options.text: Changing the type of the `price` field in a response from string to number
options.why: Changing a type makes the client parse or compare wrongly. It looks small, but it is breaking.

options.text: Adding a new field called `avatarUrl` to the response
options.why: Old clients ignore fields they don't know, so this is a safe additive change.

options.text: Requiring a new mandatory `couponCode` field in the request
options.why: Old clients don't send this field, so every request they make now gets a 422.

options.text: Creating a new `GET /api/v1/offers` endpoint
options.why: Nobody was calling it before, so nothing breaks for anyone.

questions.q: Ryan's app has two clients: a Vue web app that deploys together with the API, and a mobile app that stays in use for up to six months after a release. He wants to rename the `name` field. What is the safest path?
questions.hint: Do you have any control over when the mobile app updates?

options.text: Rename name to fullName in one deploy, since the web app is fine
options.why: Old versions of the mobile app will look for name and find nothing. The web app being fine isn't enough.

options.text: Send both fields for a while, and after clients have moved over, remove the old one with a deprecation
options.why: With both name and fullName present, old and new clients both work. Then you can retire the old one gradually.

options.text: Email mobile users asking them to update, then rename
options.why: There's no guarantee everyone will update. Some people stay on an old app for months.

options.text: Rename it without bumping the version, and just write a changelog entry
options.why: Nobody reads the changelog, and an old app's code certainly doesn't.

questions.q: In the routes configuration below, which controller runs when v2 is called?
questions.code:
api_v1:
    resource: ../src/Controller/Api/V1/
    type: attribute
    prefix: /api/v1

api_v2:
    resource: ../src/Controller/Api/V2/
    type: attribute
    prefix: /api/v2
questions.hint: What prefix is given next to each folder?

options.text: The controllers in `src/Controller/Api/V2/`, with routes starting at /api/v2
options.why: The resource folder and the prefix together create the v2 routes. v1 stays separate.

options.text: The controllers in `src/Controller/Api/V1/`, because v1 was written first
options.why: Routes are matched by prefix, not by order. /api/v2/... only matches routes from the V2 folder.

options.text: Neither, because the attribute type only wants a prefix on the controller itself
options.why: Loading attribute routes from a folder in routes.yaml and giving them a prefix is valid and common.

options.text: Both controllers run together
options.why: Each request matches exactly one route, and because the prefixes differ the two never claim the same URL.

questions.q: Which steps should you take before shutting down v1?
questions.hint: How can you find out who will break when you shut it down?

options.text: Send Deprecation and Sunset headers on v1 responses
options.why: It tells clients in code when the shutdown comes, so they can move off in time.

options.text: Count from the logs which clients still call v1
options.why: If the number isn't close to zero, shutting down means deliberately breaking some people.

options.text: Delete the route overnight with no announcement
options.why: Those still using it get no chance to find out, and they all break on the same morning.

options.text: After the shutdown date, return 410 Gone instead of 404
options.why: 410 clearly says the resource existed and was removed on purpose; a 404 sounds like a wrong URL.

questions.q: Ryan renamed a field and, in the same commit, changed the matching `name` line in the test. CI is green. What is the problem?
questions.hint: Whose expectation was the test checking, and who changed that expectation?

options.text: CI was slow and needs more tests
options.why: It isn't the number of tests. The test that was supposed to guard against the break was itself changed.

options.text: Changing the test erased the old client's expectation, so the break went unnoticed
options.why: When the same hand changes code and test, the test only verifies the new behavior. That is why clients' expectations live in a separate contract test.

options.text: He should have used Behat instead of PHPUnit for a rename
options.why: Changing the tool doesn't fix it. The problem is that the list of expectations changes along with the code.

options.text: There is no problem, because the new name is clearer
options.why: The name may be clearer, but old clients don't recognize it, and that is exactly why contracts exist.

questions.q: Ryan's company has web, iOS, Android and smart TV apps on one backend. Each screen needs something different, and with REST he has to build a separate endpoint for each. Which style fixes this pain?
questions.hint: Who decides which fields come back: the server or the client?

options.text: gRPC, because it is the fastest
options.why: Speed isn't the pain here. And bringing gRPC straight to TV or browser clients is hard too.

options.text: GraphQL, where each client writes out the fields it needs
options.why: Each client asks one general endpoint for the shape it needs, so there is no need for separate endpoints.

options.text: Async messages, because the client doesn't wait
options.why: A screen needs its data right now. A message doesn't give you an immediate answer.

options.text: No style change; let every client accept the same response
options.why: Over-fetching and under-fetching would carry on, and the pain would grow.

questions.q: What is wrong with the response of POST /reports in the code below?
questions.hint: Has the report really been built at this moment?

options.text: The work is running in the background, yet the response says done and 200. The client will be misled
options.why: For unfinished work you should return 202 with status pending, plus a Location header.

options.text: It is wrong to flush before calling dispatch
options.why: Flushing first is actually correct. Otherwise the worker wouldn't find the report row in the database.

options.text: The controller should build the report itself, without Messenger
options.why: That would make the user sit for 20 seconds, and could time out as well.

options.text: It should return HTML instead of JSON
options.why: The format isn't the problem. The problem is lying about the state of the work.

questions.q: In which of these cases is gRPC a good choice?
questions.hint: Do you control both sides, and who is calling?

options.text: Thousands of calls per second between two internal Symfony services
options.why: Both sides are yours, Protobuf is compact and HTTP/2 is fast. Typed code reduces mistakes too.

options.text: Giving a small outside partner a simple API to try with curl
options.why: A binary format isn't easy to try with curl. REST is the straightforward choice here.

options.text: Sharing a .proto file between services in two different languages (PHP and Go) to keep a typed contract
options.why: Code for each language can be generated from the .proto, so the contract lives in one place.

options.text: Directly from a Vue app in the browser, with no proxy
options.why: A browser can't speak native gRPC. You need gRPC-Web or a proxy in between.

questions.q: A small blog app: one Vue frontend, one Symfony API, a team of three. Someone proposes adding GraphQL, "because everyone does it now". What is the best answer?
questions.hint: What was the pain?

options.text: Good idea, GraphQL is always better than REST
options.why: Not better or worse, just different. Without the pain, extra complexity is only cost.

options.text: First let's check whether we really have over-fetching or repeated calls. If not, REST is right
options.why: With one client and a small team this pain is usually almost absent, while GraphQL brings caching and security complexity.

options.text: If we add GraphQL we should add gRPC too, so we have every style
options.why: The more styles you have, the heavier the burden of running and learning them.

options.text: REST is right, because GraphQL never works in production
options.why: GraphQL runs at many large companies. The question is whether this app needs it.

questions.q: The payment team renames `total` to `amount` in its JSON reply. Next day every order in the order service shows $0, and no error is logged. What would have caught this before deploy?
questions.hint: Where does the contract live, and who checks it?

options.text: A shared .proto file with generated clients, so the old field name stops existing in CI
options.why: Both sides generate code from the same file, so the rename breaks the build or static analysis, not production.

options.text: A longer timeout on the HTTP call
options.why: The call succeeded. The data was read wrongly, so timing is not the issue.

options.text: Writing `?? null` instead of `?? 0`
options.why: Still silent: the key is missing either way and nothing tells you the contract changed.

options.text: Moving the payment service to a message queue
options.why: A queue changes how the message travels, not who checks its shape.

questions.q: Why is caching harder in GraphQL than in REST?
questions.hint: What does an HTTP cache build its cache key from?

options.text: GraphQL usually talks through POST to a single URL, so HTTP caching by URL doesn't work
options.why: In REST every resource has its own URL and a GET, so browsers and CDNs cache it easily.

options.text: GraphQL responses are always encrypted
options.why: Encryption has nothing to do with it; the reason is the URL and the method.

options.text: Database queries are slower in GraphQL
options.why: Database speed doesn't depend on the style. Caching is harder because of the shape of the request.

options.text: Caching GraphQL is forbidden
options.why: It isn't forbidden, but you have to do it differently, on the server or in the client library.

questions.q: An admin panel pages through a list of 2 million orders with `OFFSET`. Pages near the end take 5 seconds. What is the most correct fix?
questions.hint: What is the real cause of the slowness: the rows skipped, or the rows returned?

options.text: Add RAM to the server
options.why: More RAM may help a little, but the cost of skipping extra rows on every deeper page stays.

options.text: Move to cursor (keyset) pagination, so the index reaches the spot after the last row directly
options.why: It skips no rows, goes straight to the spot and picks up 20, so every page is equally fast.

options.text: Reduce the page size from 20 to 10
options.why: Smaller pages mean more pages, and the skipped rows of OFFSET only go deeper.

options.text: Run COUNT(*) every time to work out the last page
options.why: COUNT is itself slow on a big table, and it doesn't fix the OFFSET problem.

questions.q: What is wrong with the code below?
questions.hint: What happens when many orders come in during the same second?

options.text: limit + 1 in setMaxResults is wrong; it should be just limit
options.why: limit + 1 is right. It tells you whether there are more pages.

options.text: There is no tie-breaker (id), so rows with the same createdAt get lost at the page boundary
options.why: The condition `< :at` drops rows with an equal value. You need to add id to both the ordering and the condition.

options.text: DESC ordering doesn't work with cursor pagination
options.why: DESC works fine. You just have to match the direction of the condition (<) to the ordering.

options.text: You can't do keyset with QueryBuilder, you need native SQL
options.why: You can do it easily with QueryBuilder, with the condition spelled out using OR.

questions.q: In which of these cases is offset pagination still a fine choice?
questions.hint: How big is the list, and does the user jump straight to a page number?

options.text: A fixed list of the 64 districts of the country, and the user wants to go to "page 3"
options.why: A small, stable list: the cost of OFFSET is negligible, and jumping to a page number is easy.

options.text: A timeline of 100 million rows with new rows arriving every second
options.why: Here very deep pages and shifting rows are both problems. You need a cursor.

options.text: An admin report of a few hundred rows, where "jump to page 5" is needed
options.why: Small size, and page numbers are needed. For simplicity, offset is fine.

options.text: An infinite-scroll feed in a mobile app
options.why: A feed changes constantly, and no jumping is needed beyond "next". A cursor is the natural fit.

questions.q: A Vue app opens every cursor and sorts its own list by the created_at inside. What is the future risk?
questions.hint: Whose job is it to decide the structure of the cursor?

options.text: No risk, because the cursor's structure never changes
options.why: If the server changes the ordering (say adding a new column next to id), the structure can change.

options.text: The client will break when the server changes the structure; the cursor should stay opaque
options.why: If the cursor is an opaque token, the server is free to change its insides.

options.text: The cursor will get too long and break the URL
options.why: The cursor is short, and that is not the main risk either.

options.text: Browsers can't read base64
options.why: Browsers can. The problem isn't technical, it is about who is responsible for what.

questions.q: Which index helps most for the condition (created_at, id) < (:at, :id) in Postgres?
questions.hint: The column order of the index has to match the ORDER BY.

options.text: On id alone
options.why: Even with an index on id, sorting and filtering by created_at still need a separate sort.

options.text: On created_at alone
options.why: To order rows with an equal created_at, the database has to do extra work.

options.text: A composite index on the two columns (created_at, id)
options.why: It matches the order of both the ORDER BY and the WHERE, so the database follows the index straight to the spot after the last row.

options.text: A separate index on each column, so both are there
options.why: Two separate indexes can't be used fully for a paired condition. A composite index is the right one.

questions.q: The Vue app retries a timed-out payment with a key made inside the retry loop, so each attempt gets a fresh UUID. What happens?
questions.hint: How does the server decide that two requests are the same payment?

options.text: Nothing is fixed: every attempt looks like a new payment, so the customer can still be charged twice
options.why: The key only works when it is shared by all attempts of one payment. Make it once, before the loop.

options.text: The server rejects every retry with a 409
options.why: A new key looks like a brand-new payment, so the server happily processes it.

options.text: It is safe, because a UUID is unique and that is what idempotency needs
options.why: Uniqueness per attempt is exactly the problem. The server needs the same key to recognize a repeat.

options.text: The retry is skipped because POST is never retried
options.why: canRetry allows POST when an idempotency key exists, which is the point of having one.

questions.q: What is wrong with the response in the code below?
questions.hint: To monitoring, caching and client code, does this look like a success or a failure?

options.text: It uses 200 for a failure, and the message is meaningless
options.why: If the status lies, every tool goes the wrong way. It should have been a correct 4xx, with the reason given by a fixed code.

options.text: Using json() is wrong, it should use Response
options.why: json() is fine. The problem is the quality of the status and the message.

options.text: findByEmail is slow
options.why: Speed isn't the issue here, the shape of the error response is.

options.text: There is no problem, because the client will understand from the body
options.why: Tools don't read the body, they look at the status. And the client learns nothing from "error" either.

questions.q: A user is logged in but is trying to open someone else's order. What is the most correct status?
questions.hint: Does the server know who they are?

options.text: 401 Unauthorized
options.why: 401 means the identity is unknown. Here the identity is known and the permission is missing.

options.text: 403 Forbidden (or 404, to hide that it exists)
options.why: The identity is known but there is no permission, hence 403. If you want to keep the order's existence secret, a 404 is acceptable too.

options.text: 500 Internal Server Error
options.why: This isn't a server mistake, it is a lack of permission on the client's side.

options.text: 200 OK, with "no permission" in the body
options.why: If you return 200 for a failure, the tools assume everything is fine.

questions.q: In which of these cases may the client retry automatically?
questions.hint: Could sending again change the result? And does doing it twice do harm?

options.text: GET /products returned 503
options.why: GET is idempotent, and 503 is temporary. Retrying with backoff is safe.

options.text: POST /register returned 422
options.why: 422 means the input is wrong. Sending it again without fixing it gets the same answer.

options.text: PUT /profile/7 timed out
options.why: PUT is idempotent. Even if it runs twice, the profile ends up in the same state.

options.text: POST /payments timed out and there is no idempotency key
options.why: It is unknown whether the job was done, and if it runs twice the money is charged twice. Retrying without a key is dangerous.

questions.q: Ryan's Vue app wants to show the right message beside the email input when it gets a validation error. What is most useful to have in the response?
questions.hint: How will the client know which input has which mistake?

options.text: Just one message: "Form invalid"
options.why: The client doesn't know which input is wrong. It can only show a generic message everywhere.

options.text: An `errors` list: each mistake's field, fixed code and message
options.why: The client uses the field to put the message beside the right input, and the code to decide the behavior.

options.text: Only the message of the first mistake
options.why: The user fixes it, resends and gets stuck on the second mistake, going round and round.

options.text: A stack trace, so the developer can understand
options.why: A stack trace is no use to the user, and it creates a security risk too.

questions.q: Why does the API's error response carry both `"code": "stock_insufficient"` and `"detail": "Only 2 in stock"`, and not just detail?
questions.hint: What happens to the client's code when the wording of detail changes?

options.text: You could drop detail, the code alone is enough
options.why: People and debugging need detail. The two have different jobs.

options.text: detail can change, so client code reads the fixed code. detail is for people
options.why: If the language or wording changes, code that depends on detail breaks. The code is part of the contract, so it stays fixed.

options.text: They do the same job, it is only extra safety
options.why: Safety has nothing to do with it; it is about stability and readability.

options.text: RFC 9457 says so, and there is no need to know why
options.why: The RFC gives the mould, and if you understand the reason you will use it properly.

questions.q: A partner's script is calling the API 30 times a second, and every other user is suffering slowness. What is the most correct remedy?
questions.hint: The problem is one party's load, not the others'.

options.text: Give each client (each API key) its own rate limit, so that if one does too much, only that one is blocked
options.why: When the limit is per key, the damage stays with that one client, and the others carry on as normal.

options.text: Add more servers
options.why: The loop can fire even more requests. Without a limit, however many servers you add, one person's mistake will eat them all.

options.text: One general limit for the whole API: 1000 a minute in total
options.why: Then the loop uses up all 1000, and ordinary users get no share of it. The limit has to be per separate key.

options.text: Email the partner to fix the script, and do nothing else
options.why: Emailing is good, but if you don't protect your own system, the same thing will happen next time.

questions.q: What do `limit` and `rate` separately set in the config below?
questions.code:
api_per_client:
    policy: 'token_bucket'
    limit: 100
    rate: { interval: '1 minute', amount: 20 }
questions.hint: One is the size of the bucket, the other is the refill speed.

options.text: The bucket holds at most 100 tokens (burst), and refills 20 a minute (the average rate)
options.why: limit is the burst ceiling, rate is the refill speed. Two separate numbers.

options.text: 100 requests a minute and 20 a second
options.why: The interval of rate is a minute, not a second. And limit doesn't mention any time.

options.text: They are the same thing, written two ways
options.why: One is a size and the other a speed. If they weren't separate, you couldn't set the burst and the average independently.

options.text: 100 requests in total a day, and 20 a minute
options.why: There is no mention of a day here. Counting over days or months is a quota, not the rate limiter.

questions.q: The listener below keys the limit on the raw X-Api-Key header. How can a scripted client get around the limit?
questions.hint: What does each new key value get?

options.text: Send a different made-up X-Api-Key on every request, so each one lands in a fresh, full bucket
options.why: The header is never checked, and every distinct key has its own bucket. Verify the key before using it.

options.text: Send the requests more slowly than the refill rate
options.why: That is just obeying the limit, not getting around it.

options.text: Use a very long header value so the limiter overflows
options.why: The key length does not change how the bucket is counted.

options.text: It can't, because the limit also applies to the IP
options.why: The IP is used only when the header is missing, so sending any header value skips it.

questions.q: A client gets a 429 and sees `Retry-After: 3`. What should it do?
questions.hint: Has the server said anything itself?

options.text: Send again immediately, maybe it will work this time
options.why: The limit is still exceeded. Sending again just gets another 429 and more load on the server.

options.text: Wait about 3 seconds (with a little jitter) and send again
options.why: The server told you the time itself. Jitter keeps many clients from returning at once.

options.text: Show the user "failed" and stop, no retry
options.why: The limit is temporary and it will work in a moment. Showing the user a failure for no reason isn't right (for idempotent work).

options.text: Create a new API key to get around the limit
options.why: That is dodging the limit, and it breaks the terms of service.

questions.q: For which of these reasons is it better to avoid an IP-based rate limit, or to pair it with another key?
questions.hint: How many people can there be behind one IP?

options.text: A mobile carrier sends thousands of users out through the same public IP
options.why: One person's fault blocks the requests of thousands.

options.text: Behind a load balancer without trusted_proxies set right, everyone's IP looks the same
options.why: getClientIp() returns the load balancer's IP, so everyone is counted as one person.

options.text: Because an IP is short
options.why: That has nothing to do with setting a limit.

options.text: For logged-in users, the user id is fairer
options.why: When you count per person, one person's behavior doesn't affect another.

questions.q: To stop password guessing, which measure for the `/login` endpoint makes the most sense?
questions.hint: How should the limit compare with an ordinary API's?

options.text: The same limit as the ordinary API (100 a minute), to keep it simple
options.why: 100 password guesses a minute is far too many chances. Login needs a strict limit.

options.text: A separate strict limiter, such as 5 tries in 15 minutes (sliding window), by IP and email
options.why: Brute force slows to a crawl, while an ordinary user's normal mistakes are tolerated.

options.text: No limit, just demand strong passwords
options.why: Strong passwords are good, but without a limit an attacker can fire millions of guesses.

options.text: Sleep for 5 seconds on every request
options.why: It slows everybody down, and an attacker can get around it by firing many requests at once.

questions.q: What is the biggest problem in the code below?
questions.hint: What happens if someone opens the browser's DevTools and changes `total`?

options.text: The total and discount sent by the client are trusted directly, so anyone can set whatever price they like
options.why: Price and discount should be the server's calculation. The client should send only the product id and quantity.

options.text: toArray() is slow, json_decode() is faster
options.why: The speed difference is negligible. The big problems are security and where the rules live.

options.text: Passing the user to the Order constructor is wrong
options.why: Attaching the order's owner is correct. The problem is total and discount.

options.text: setDiscount() should be called before setTotal()
options.why: Changing the order fixes nothing, the main problem is the source.

questions.q: Kevin's phone costs $500 with a 10% discount. A user sends `{"items": [{"productId": 42, "quantity": 1}], "total": 1}` to the checkout controller above. What total is stored?
questions.hint: Does the request class have a `total` field?

options.text: $450, calculated by the server from the database price and the discount rule
options.why: The client's total is never read. The Quote is built from the real price ($500) minus 10%.

options.text: 1 cent, because the client sent it
options.why: That was the old code. Here no client-controlled value reaches the price.

options.text: $500, because the server ignores the discount for API calls
options.why: The discount rule lives in DiscountPolicy and applies to every caller, web, mobile or direct.

options.text: An error, because the JSON has an unexpected field
options.why: The serializer ignores fields the request class does not declare, so the call succeeds with the real price.

questions.q: Which of these jobs can safely stay in the client?
questions.hint: Which is only display and convenience, and which is a business decision?

options.text: Formatting money and dates for display
options.why: This is only presentation. A wrong format looks bad, but doesn't harm the business.

options.text: An up-front check on the email field, so the user catches mistakes quickly
options.why: Fine for convenience, but the real validation must still exist on the server.

options.text: Calculating how much a coupon code takes off
options.why: The discount is a business rule. In the client it gets duplicated and can be altered.

options.text: The final decision on whether the user may cancel the order
options.why: Permission is the server's decision. The client only shows a button from the server's flag.

questions.q: A Vue app shows the cancel button with `v-if="order.status === 'placed' && order.ownerId === me.id"`. Ryan says, "The server has the rule too, so there is no problem." What is the best answer?
questions.hint: In how many places is the rule written?

options.text: That's fine, because having the rule in two places makes it safer
options.why: When the rule changes, the two places will drift apart. Security comes from the server's check, not from a duplicate rule.

options.text: Keep the rule in the server's Voter and send an `abilities.cancel` flag in the response; Vue just looks at the flag
options.why: The rule is written once, and when it changes the client stays the same. The server runs the Voter again on the real action too.

options.text: The client's rule is fine, throw away the server's Voter
options.why: Without a check on the server, anyone can call the API directly and cancel.

options.text: Always show the button, and the server will say "no" on click
options.why: It is safe, but shows the user a pointless failure. With a flag the UX stays good too.

questions.q: After building separate BFFs for mobile and web, someone proposes: "Let's put the discount calculation in the mobile BFF, so the core service stays small." What do you say?
questions.hint: What happens if the web BFF doesn't have the discount calculation?

options.text: Right, the BFF is just for mobile anyway
options.why: If the rule is in the mobile BFF, you will have to write it separately in the web BFF, and prices won't match again.

options.text: No. The rules stay in the core service; the BFF only changes the shape
options.why: When business rules are in one place, every client and every BFF gets the same answer.

options.text: Drop the BFF and let mobile go straight to the database
options.why: Going straight to the database is dangerous for both security and rules.

options.text: Copying the discount calculation into both BFFs is fine, just be careful
options.why: Copied code drifts apart when it changes, and being careful can't prevent that.

questions.q: A partner calls your API directly and uses neither your Vue app nor your mobile app. What would happen to them if the business rules lived in the client?
questions.hint: Does your client code ever reach the partner?

options.text: Nothing, because the partner would write their own rules
options.why: Then you have separate rules again, and prices wouldn't match. That is exactly the problem.

options.text: The rules would never reach them, so they would get the wrong price or permissions
options.why: The client's code only runs in your apps. With the rules on the server, the partner gets the same answer.

options.text: The partner would automatically run the Vue app's code
options.why: A partner only calls the API over HTTP and runs no client code.

options.text: A rate limit would solve it
options.why: A rate limit is for a different problem (load). It doesn't fill the gap of missing rules.
